questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A lost update from two threads
questions.learningObjective: trace a read-modify-write across two threads and name the update that disappears
questions.stem: A shared balance field holds 100 and no lock guards it. Thread T1 reads the balance into a local, adds 10, and is paused before it stores the result. Thread T2 reads the same 100, adds 20, and stores 120. T1 then resumes and stores 110. Which update has been lost?

options.text: T2's deposit of 20, because T1's store of 110 overwrote the 120 that T2 had already written
Neither update, because both threads read and then wrote a value derived from the same 100
options.misconception: assumes two stores derived from one read both survive

options.text: T1's deposit of 10, because the field ended lower than the 120 that T2 had written
options.misconception: reads a lower final value as proof the first writer lost

options.text: Both updates, because a field written twice can only hold one of the two values
options.misconception: believes two stores to one field always discard both

questions.explanation: Each thread computed a value from the 100 it read, and only one of those two computed values can be in the field at the end, so one deposit is gone. T1's store lands second and overwrites the 120 that T2 had already committed, which destroys T2's work even though T2 ran to completion and reported success. The whole failure sits in the gap between the read and the store: the guarantee that is missing is that no other thread may write between this thread's read and its store. A field that is only ever written with a value derived from a fresh read needs no lock, and this field is not that.
questions.hint: Ask what each thread had read at the moment it computed the value it stored.

questions.topic: Why a read-modify-write is not one step
questions.learningObjective: explain what the guarantee covers when a value is read, changed and stored
questions.stem: Adding 1 to a counter is written as three lines: read the field, add one to what was read, store the field. The three lines are often described as one operation. Why is that description unsafe when two threads run them?

options.text: The three lines are three separate events on shared state, and a thread can be paused between any two of them
The three lines are each indivisible, and a pause can only happen after all three have finished
options.misconception: believes each line is indivisible and so the pair is too

options.text: Only the read is dangerous, because a store always writes the value the thread intended to write
options.misconception: blames the read alone and trusts the store

options.text: Only a wide counter is dangerous, because a narrow value can be read and stored in one step
options.misconception: thinks a wider value is what makes the update unsafe

questions.explanation: The name one operation hides three points at which control can change hands, and the interesting gap is between the read and the store. What the code actually guarantees is that this thread stored the value it computed; it guarantees nothing about what any other thread did to the field in between, which is exactly where the update is lost. A guarantee that no other thread may write between a read and a store has to be provided by something outside these three lines, such as a lock held across all of them or a single indivisible instruction. Describing the sequence as one operation is how the missing guarantee stays invisible in review.
questions.hint: Ask how many separate shared-state events the three lines are.

options.misconception: counts what survives in the field rather than how many callers acted

options.misconception: assumes a single field can admit only one successful caller

options.misconception: assumes a later pass repairs the decision the first pass got wrong

questions.learningObjective: name what a lock held across a slow call makes wait
questions.stem: A routine takes a lock, reads a row over the network, writes the row back, and only then releases the lock. The read takes 400 milliseconds. Two requests arrive at the same instant. What has the lock made the second request wait for?

options.text: The whole first critical section, because the second cannot begin its read until the first releases the lock
Only the 400 millisecond read, since the write that follows needs no lock of its own
options.misconception: believes the trailing write sits outside the critical section

options.text: Nothing, because the two requests read different rows and the lock guards only the connection
options.misconception: assumes a different row makes the two requests independent

options.text: Half the critical section, because the lock is dropped as soon as the read returns a row
options.misconception: believes the lock is released part way through the body

questions.explanation: The lock covers the read and the write, so everything between taking it and releasing it is time in which no other caller may enter. The second request therefore waits 500 milliseconds, the whole of the first critical section, before its own read even starts. A lock does not know which parts of the body are slow, so moving a 400 millisecond call inside it converts that call into 400 milliseconds of blocked time for every other caller. Holding the lock only around the final store would have been correct for the row and would have let the two reads overlap, finishing the pair in 800 milliseconds rather than 1000.

The remote call is slower in this environment than in the tests, since 450 ms is well above its usual figure
options.misconception: blames the dependency for time the lock itself added

options.text: Eight threads is more than this routine can use, since fewer threads would give the same slow responses
options.misconception: blames the thread count for waiting time a lock caused

questions.topic: Two locks taken in opposite orders
questions.learningObjective: recognise the deadlock that opposite lock orders create
questions.stem: One routine takes the account lock and then the ledger lock. Another takes the ledger lock and then the account lock. Two threads call one routine each at the same moment, and the first thread takes its first lock before the second thread takes its first lock. What happens?

options.text: Each thread holds one lock and waits for the other, so neither can finish and the pair is deadlocked
Both finish, because the waiting threads are served in the order in which they began waiting
options.misconception: assumes waiting for a lock queues in arrival order

options.text: Only the ledger routine fails, since the account lock is the one taken first in the other routine
options.misconception: believes one of the two orders is inherently the correct one

options.text: Both finish, because a thread that cannot get its second lock gives back the one it already holds
options.misconception: assumes a blocked thread releases what it already holds

questions.explanation: Each thread now holds the single lock the other one needs next, and neither will release what it holds until the body finishes, so neither body can finish. Waiting for a lock is not a queue: a waiting thread keeps everything it already holds, which is why the two can hold each other up indefinitely. The guarantee that would prevent this is a single agreed order in which every routine takes multiple locks, so that a thread always waits for a lock no other thread is holding while it waits. Opposite orders pass every test that runs the routines one at a time, because with one thread the first routine always completes before the second begins.

One thread runs transferOut and another runs transferIn, and each acquires its first lock before the other thread acquires any. What does the program print?

Both transfers complete, because two separate locks cannot interfere with each other
options.misconception: believes distinct locks are always independent of one another

options.text: One line from transferOut, because that thread takes the account lock first
options.misconception: assumes taking a lock first grants a thread any second lock

options.text: One line from each, because a blocked thread still runs the statements after the wait
options.misconception: believes statements after a blocking lock still execute

questions.stem: A test suite runs two transfer routines on a single thread and passes 200 consecutive times. The staging environment runs eight workers, and in about one run out of two hundred the service stopped answering until it was restarted. The log records no exception and no timeout. What does this evidence support?

options.text: A fault that needs a particular order of the two threads, which a test that runs them one at a time cannot reach
A memory leak, since the only difference between the two environments is how long the service ran
options.misconception: reads an unexplained hang as evidence about memory

options.misconception: attributes a permanent hang to a slow remote call

questions.stem: To remove the fault between the two transfer routines, a team replaces both locks with a single lock guarding every account and ledger change. The fault goes away and the code is shorter. What has the team given up to get that?

Only the fault itself, because a single lock leaves no second lock for a thread to wait on

options.text: The safety of the transfers, because one lock cannot protect two different records at the same time
options.misconception: believes a lock is bound to a single record

options.text: Nothing worth naming, because the two locks already had every caller waiting its turn
options.misconception: believes the two old locks already serialised all callers

That is a real trade rather than a free improvement, and it is invisible in the diff because the code got simpler. The alternative that keeps the concurrency is one agreed order in which the two routines take both locks, which is more code and no loss of parallelism.

questions.topic: Why a barrier and a latch are not the same thing
questions.learningObjective: explain the difference in what a barrier and a latch wait for
questions.stem: Six workers each process one part of an input and then combine their parts into a single result. The team must also let four waiting tasks start only once every part is in place. answer.exemplar: A latch counts down and opens once, permanently, when a set number of arrivals is reached: threads wait to be let through and then carry on, and nothing goes back. A barrier counts arrivals and then releases everyone at once, but the participants that passed through are expected to come back for the next round, so a second phase can wait on the same barrier. The six workers combining their parts need a barrier, because every worker must arrive before any of them can proceed and all six will be needed again. The four waiting tasks need a latch, because they are waiting to be released once and have no part in the next stage. Using a latch for the combine means the first worker to arrive opens it and the others find it already open.

The distinction is about what happens after the wait, not about how long anyone waits: both are waits on a count, and both are invisible in code that uses only one of them. The failure that shows up when they are confused is silent, because an open latch releases latecomers immediately, so a worker that took a slow path simply proceeds without the parts it needed and the combined result is quietly wrong rather than obviously broken. A barrier knows how many participants to expect, which is why it can be reused and a latch cannot.

questions.stem: A pool has 4 workers. Ten tasks are submitted at the same instant and each task takes 1.5 seconds. A worker takes the next task the moment it becomes free, and the tasks are taken in the order submitted. At what time does the last of the ten tasks start?
questions.explanation: Four workers take the first four tasks at once, the next four at 1.5 seconds, and the last two at 3 seconds, so the tenth task starts at 3; counting the waves as 3 minus 1 and multiplying by 1.5 gives the same figure. The queue drains in waves rather than smoothly, because the workers were all freed at the same instant, and that is why a pool's last task can start much later than an average of the task times would suggest. The number is also the honest measure of what submitting 10 tasks at once costs: the caller continues immediately, and the work still has to happen, so the wait has been moved to the pool's queue where only its length shows it.
questions.hint: Count the full waves of four before the last task, then multiply by the task time.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a failure returned on a limit does not say
questions.learningObjective: explain why a limit failure cannot report whether the work took effect
questions.stem: A caller gives a write a 2 second limit. The write takes 3 seconds on the far side. The caller receives a failure and tells the user nothing was saved, and 2 seconds later the write completes. Explain why the failure tells the caller so little, and what a caller has to be given before it can act on it.

answer.exemplar: The limit ends the caller's wait, not the work: the write is already under way on the far side and nothing in the failure reaches it, so at the moment the caller is told 'nothing saved' the write may yet succeed, may still fail, and may already have partly applied. The failure is evidence about the reply, not about the record, and the caller cannot tell which of the three it is in. So a caller needs a way to ask afterwards what happened: an identifier it supplied and the far side recorded, so the retry or the query returns the outcome of the first attempt rather than starting a second. The alternative is to not accept the ambiguity at all, by making the call's completion knowable — a receipt the caller can look up, or refusing writes that cannot be answered inside the limit.

questions.explanation: A complete answer says the limit governs the caller's wait and has no reach into work already under way, that the caller is therefore being told about the reply rather than the record, and that it needs a recorded identifier from the first attempt to find out what happened. The tempting answer is that the far side should honour the limit by abandoning the write, which would make the failure meaningful, and it is usually the wrong trade: a write abandoned part way through is the same half-applied state this question is about, and it trades a confusing failure for a corrupted record. The other tempting answer is to retry straight away, which is the behaviour that turns one ambiguous outcome into two, since the first attempt may still complete after the second has already been issued.
questions.hint: Ask whether the failure is evidence about the reply or about the record.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A suite that only fails where it is threaded
questions.learningObjective: read an environment difference that changes what a test can reach
questions.stem: The same suite passes on a developer machine that runs the code on one thread. In staging, which runs eight workers, it passes too, and once in about three hundred runs the two threads that share a lock pair stop responding. What does the difference between the two environments tell you?

options.text: The single-threaded machine cannot set up the arrangement at all, so its passes are not evidence about it
The staging workers are the cause, since eight of them is more than the code was written for
options.misconception: blames the worker count for a fault two threads can also reach

options.text: The developer machine is wrong, since a routine that can hang must also fail when run once
options.misconception: believes a single-threaded run can reproduce a two-thread fault

options.text: Nothing yet, because three hundred runs is too few to draw a conclusion from
options.misconception: dismisses a reproducible rate as too small a sample

questions.explanation: The two environments differ in exactly the property the fault depends on, so the clean passes on one thread and the hang on eight are the same code behaving as written for each. A thread that runs the routines in sequence always releases its locks before the next begins, which is why the state in which each thread holds what the other wants is never reached, and no number of single-threaded passes will change that. The last option is worth taking seriously for the wrong faults and dismissing for this one: three hundred runs is plenty to establish a rate, and a rate near one in three hundred is what a rare interleaving looks like rather than what noise looks like. The fix for the evidence is a test that uses two threads, not more repetitions of one that cannot reach the arrangement.
questions.hint: Ask what the single-threaded machine is structurally unable to set up.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a republished snapshot costs per second
questions.learningObjective: compute the per-second cost of copying a shared value on a fixed schedule
questions.stem: A shared map of 40000 entries is made safe by copying it and publishing the copy. A background thread republishes it every 200 milliseconds whether or not anything changed. How many entry copies does that thread perform each second?
questions.explanation: Five republishes a second at 40000 entries each is 200000 entry copies a second, and 40000 times 1000 divided by 200 gives the same figure. That is the standing price of the arrangement, paid whether or not a single entry changed, which is the part a design review should weigh: the cost is a function of the schedule and the size, not of the traffic. It stays invisible in a test because a test that changes nothing and reads from the published copy sees correct results throughout, and it shows up in production as a background thread holding a core for no reason. Copying on change rather than on a timer removes the standing cost and leaves only the cost of the changes that actually happen.
questions.hint: Work out how many republications fall in a second, then multiply by the entries copied each time.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a queue can hide a failing consumer for hours
questions.learningObjective: explain how a buffer delays the appearance of a rate mismatch
questions.stem: A service's response times stayed flat for six hours while its consumer ran at half speed, and the first sign of trouble was one host being killed for using all its memory. Explain how the arrangement hid the mismatch for so long, and what would have shown it earlier.

answer.exemplar: The queue absorbed the difference: the producer's cost was the put and the return, neither of which grows, so every response-time measurement stayed at its old value while five extra entries a second went in and one out. Nothing in the response path could see the length, because the length is a property of the buffer and the buffer is not on the path a response travels. The first honest signal was therefore a resource limit, and a resource limit is a bad signal because it names the host rather than the cause and arrives with no measure of how long it had been building. Earlier visibility comes from the queue's own length, charted next to the rates: the length is the quantity actually growing, and it grows from the first second. Alerting on the length, or on the gap between the two rates, would have turned a six-hour memory climb into a one-minute graph.

questions.explanation: A complete answer says the queue absorbed the difference so the response path never changed, that the growing quantity was the queue's length rather than anything a response reports, and that charting the length or the rate gap is what would have exposed it from the first second. The tempting answer is that the dashboard was wrong, which is too shallow: it was measuring the part of the system that genuinely was not changing, which is a common and specific kind of blind spot. The second tempting answer is that the fix is a bigger queue, and it inverts the finding, because a longer queue would have extended the period in which nothing was visible rather than shortened it. A bound on the queue converts the same mismatch into a delay at the producer, where a response time can finally report it.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity was growing, and whether anything on the response path could see it.
